books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”
Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, B. Cotton, Slavery, and the Southern Exception

stimulus.text: A summary of the 1840 census: about one in three white families in the slave states owned enslaved people. In South Carolina, nearly half of white families owned slaves. Most slaveholders owned few enslaved people: about half held fewer than five, and nearly nine in ten held fewer than twenty. Only a small number held more than one hundred.
stimulus.source_note: Figures from the 1840 census: about one in three white families in the slave states owned enslaved people, South Carolina 48%, and the distribution of holdings from the census returns. Checked against Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.13 A, which states that the majority of white Southerners owned no slaves.

source: original; data summary from the 1840 United States census
stem: The figures show that most slaveholders held fewer than twenty enslaved people, and only a few held more than one hundred. What does that distribution show?

options.text: Every white family in the South owned the same number of slaves
options.misconception: The figures show a wide range, from fewer than five to more than one hundred.

options.text: Slaveholding ranged from small holders to a few very large planters
No white Southerner owned more than twenty enslaved people
options.misconception: The figures say a small number held more than one hundred.

options.text: Large planters owned no enslaved people at all
options.misconception: Large planters owned the most enslaved people, not none.

rationales.A: The figures show a wide range, from fewer than five to more than one hundred.
rationales.B: About half of holders owned fewer than five, most owned fewer than twenty, and only a few owned more than one hundred.
rationales.C: The figures say a small number held more than one hundred.
rationales.D: Large planters owned the most enslaved people, not none.
rationales.general:
1. Read the middle. About half of holders owned fewer than five enslaved people.
2. Read the top. Only a small number held more than one hundred.
3. Name the shape. Most holders were small, and a few planters held very large numbers.
Background: The famous image of the great planter covers only the top of this range.
Remember: a range is not an average; read the ends as well as the middle.
